meta.titre: Phrasal Verbs: reading, choosing and using verb-and-particle combinations
meta.sous_theme: Meaning, grammar and spotting of phrasal verbs

source.epreuve_titre: GCE A/L English Language past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: A taxi driver in Yaounde tells his passengers, "The engine has broken down, so we cannot carry on until the mechanic turns up." Every key idea in that sentence is carried by a verb and a small word that follow each other. Advanced Level papers test this pattern in two ways: grammar questions ask you to complete a sentence with the right verb-and-particle combination, and the literature or poetry paper can ask you to pick such combinations out of a stanza. A student who knows how phrasal verbs behave can do both quickly.

items: A verb is a word that shows an action or a state, and a transitive verb takes an object.
A preposition (in, on, at, to, with, of) comes before a noun or a pronoun; an adverb tells how, when or where.
A pronoun (it, him, them, me) replaces a noun.

sections.contenu_markdown:
### What a phrasal verb is

A phrasal verb is a verb followed by a particle (an adverb or a preposition). Together the two words often have a meaning that you cannot guess from the separate words: *give up* means to stop trying, and *break down* can describe a vehicle that stops working. The particle belongs to the verb. It is not a free preposition that introduces a place, as in *She walked up the hill*.

### Four patterns

| Pattern | Rule | Example |
|---|---|---|
| No object | The verb is complete without an object. | *The taxi broke down near the bridge.* |
| Object, separable | The object may stand between the verb and the particle. A pronoun object must stand there. | *They called off the match.* / *They called the match off.* / *They called it off.* |
| Object, inseparable | The object always follows the particle. | *She looks after her grandmother.* |
| Three words | Verb + adverb + preposition, never separated. | *I cannot put up with this noise.* |

### Common meanings

| Phrasal verb | Meaning |
|---|---|
| break down | stop working |
| call off | cancel |
| put off | postpone |
| turn down | refuse |
| give up | stop trying or stop a habit |
| look after | take care of |
| take after | resemble a parent or relative |
| carry on | continue |
| set off | begin a journey |
| find out | discover |
| run out of | have no more of |
| come up with | think of an idea or plan |
| put up with | tolerate |
| get over | recover from |
| look into | investigate |
| bring up | raise a child |
| turn up | arrive or appear |

### Grammar points

- The verb changes with the tense but the particle does not: *gives up, gave up, has given up, giving up*.
- In *look forward to*, the word *to* is a preposition, so a verb that follows it takes *-ing*: *I look forward to hearing from you*.
- One combination can have several meanings: *take off* describes a plane that leaves the ground and also a person who removes a cap.

variantes.nom: Spotting phrasal verbs in a text or poem
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question says pick out, identify or underline phrasal verbs
variantes.contenu_markdown: Look for a verb immediately followed by a particle, then ask whether the pair means something different from the verb alone. Test it by replacing it with a one-word verb (*carry on* can be replaced by *continue*). Write the whole combination, including the last word of a three-word verb, such as *with* in *put up with*. Do not choose a literal movement such as *climbed up the hill*. In verse, the object or another word may come between verb and particle, so read each line in normal word order before you decide.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a sentence has a blank and four options that share a verb or a particle
variantes.contenu_markdown: Work out the meaning the sentence needs, then check the grammar: tense, object, and whether the verb is separable. Options that use the same verb with different particles usually have different meanings, so eliminate them one by one by substituting the meaning of each into the sentence.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When you must rewrite a sentence with a phrasal verb, or replace a phrasal verb with one word
variantes.contenu_markdown: Keep the tense. *The board postponed the meeting* becomes *The board put off the meeting*. Remember that a pronoun object goes between verb and particle with a separable verb.

sections.enonce_markdown:
In the sentence below, choose the option that completes it correctly.

The football match was ______ because of heavy rain.

A) called on   B) called up   C) called off   D) called at

etapes.action: Read the sentence and decide what kind of word is missing.
etapes.justification: The blank follows *was* and the sentence ends with a reason, so a past participle is needed, which means a passive verb.
etapes.resultat_markdown: A passive phrasal verb: *was + past participle + particle*.

etapes.action: Predict the meaning that the sentence needs before reading the options.
etapes.justification: The match did not take place because of rain, so the missing combination means to cancel or stop something that was planned.

etapes.action: Recall the meaning of each option.
etapes.justification: *Call on* means to visit someone or to ask a person to speak. *Call up* means to telephone someone or to summon a person for service. *Call at* means to visit a place briefly. *Call off* means to cancel.
etapes.resultat_markdown: A) visit or ask; B) telephone or summon; C) cancel; D) visit a place.

etapes.justification: Only one meaning fits a match stopped by rain. Replacing the combination by *cancelled* gives *The football match was cancelled because of heavy rain*, which is logical.
etapes.resultat_markdown: A, B and D make no sense here; C fits.

etapes.action: Check the grammar of the chosen option.
etapes.justification: *Called off* is the past participle of *call off*, and *was called off* is a correct passive. The match is the thing that is cancelled, so no object is needed after *off*.
etapes.resultat_markdown: *The football match was called off because of heavy rain.*

sections.conclusion_markdown: **C) called off.** Method: predict the meaning, recall the meaning of every option, and substitute.

items.erreur_markdown: *The headmaster has looked the matter into.*
items.pourquoi_faux: *Look into* is an inseparable phrasal verb: the object must follow the particle.
items.correction_markdown: *The headmaster has looked into the matter.*

items.pourquoi_faux: With a separable phrasal verb, a pronoun object must stand between the verb and the particle.

items.erreur_markdown: *I am looking forward to meet you.*
items.pourquoi_faux: In *look forward to*, the word *to* is a preposition, so the next verb must take *-ing*.
items.correction_markdown: *I am looking forward to meeting you.*

items.erreur_markdown: *We cannot put up your behaviour any longer.*
items.pourquoi_faux: The three-word verb *put up with* has lost its last word, so the sentence does not have the meaning *tolerate*.
items.correction_markdown: *We cannot put up with your behaviour any longer.*

items.enonce_markdown:
Complete each sentence with a correct form of one phrasal verb from the box: *set off, look after, run out of, find out*.

(a) We ______ at dawn to reach Limbe before noon.
(b) Nurse Ngu will ______ the patients tonight.
(c) The shop has ______ rice, so it will order more.
(d) I want to ______ the result of the match.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **set off** (past tense: *We set off at dawn*).
(b) **look after**.
(c) **run out of** (present perfect: *has run out of rice*).
(d) **find out**.

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) Rewrite the sentence using a phrasal verb in place of the underlined word: *The committee postponed the meeting.*
(b) Rewrite your answer to (a), replacing *the meeting* with *it*.
(c) Rewrite with a phrasal verb: *The company refused his application.*
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **The committee put off the meeting** (or *put the meeting off*).
(b) **The committee put it off.** The pronoun must stand between *put* and *off*.
(c) **The company turned down his application** (or *turned his application down*).

items.enonce_markdown:
Find and correct the mistake in each sentence. One sentence is already correct; say which one.

(a) I am looking forward to see my cousin next week.
(b) She has not yet got over from the shock of the news.
(c) The students could not put up the noise any more.
(d) The headmaster looked into the complaint and promised an answer.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **seeing**: *to* is a preposition after *look forward*.
(b) Delete **from**: *got over the shock*; *get over* is already complete with its object.
(c) **put up with the noise**: the three-word verb needs *with*.
(d) **Correct**: *look into* means investigate and its object follows the particle.

items_markdown: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a particle whose meaning is often different from the meaning of the two words taken separately.
With a separable verb, a pronoun object goes between the verb and the particle (*turn it down*); with an inseparable verb the object follows (*look after her*).
Three-word phrasal verbs such as *put up with* and *run out of* must be written in full and are never separated.
After *look forward to*, use a noun or the *-ing* form, because *to* is a preposition.
To spot phrasal verbs in a poem, look for a verb plus particle that can be replaced by a one-word verb, and ignore literal movement.
In gap-fill questions, predict the meaning first, then eliminate options that share the verb but have a different particle.
